rules.name: Buy and hold
rules.rule: Hold the share the whole time.

rules.name: 200-day trend
rules.rule: Hold only while the price is above its 200-day average; otherwise cash.

rules.name: 50/200 cross
rules.rule: Hold only while the 50-day average is above the 200-day average; otherwise cash.

rules.name: 12-month momentum
rules.rule: Hold only while the price is above its level 12 months earlier; otherwise cash.

rules.name: Buy the dip
rules.rule: Buy when the 14-day RSI falls under 30; sell when it rises over 55.

rules.name: 15% trailing stop
rules.rule: Hold; sell after a 15% fall from the highest price since buying; buy back above the 50-day average.

backtests.method: Each rule decides at the close and holds over the next day. Every change of position costs 0.25% of the amount traded. Out of the market the money earns nothing. The S&P 500 fund is bought once and held over the same days. Prices are split-adjusted without dividends on both sides. The test is cut in two halves; a rule counts as beating the fund only if it is ahead in both.
limits: The tickers are today's holdings and watchlist, chosen with hindsight.
About four years of data is one market period; a rule that worked in it may not work in the next.
Dividends are left out on both sides, which slightly flatters rules that sit in cash.

doomsday.method: Each day the S&P 500 fund is given a stress level from its fall below the 12-month high, its 200-day average and its 20-day volatility. The protocol keeps 60% in the fund at Defensive and 30% at Doomsday, moves the rest to the safe asset, and steps back one level only after 10 trading days in a row at a calmer level. Each switch costs 0.25% of the amount moved. Compared with holding the fund throughout and with a plain 200-day rule (30% in the fund below the average).
doomsday.verdict: Over 23.2 years the protocol cut the worst fall from 56% to 30% and ended behind holding throughout (8.1% a year against 9.3%).

spreading.method: S&P 500 fund, every monthly starting point: all the money in on day one against six equal monthly parts, both valued twelve months after the start. Price only.

signals.method: Weekly changes in each outside series against the share's return minus the S&P 500 fund's return one to four weeks later. The history is cut in two: a lead counts only if it is clear (t-statistic of 2 or more) in the first half and shows up again with the same sign and strength in the second half. With this many tests, about the stated number would pass by luck alone.
limits: Passing this test shows a pattern in about five years of history, not a cause.
A lead that everyone can see tends to disappear once it is traded on.
Weekly data hides anything faster than a week.

rules.name: Pullback in an uptrend
rules.rule: Buy when the price is above its 200-day average and the 2-day RSI falls under 10. Sell at a close above the 5-day average, after 10 trading days, or 8% under the entry.

rules.name: Deep dip
rules.rule: Buy when the 14-day RSI falls under 30. Sell when it rises over 55, after 30 trading days, or 12% under the entry.

pct_only.label: 0.25% a trade, no minimum (your broker on trades over 450 dollars)

rules.name: Breakout
rules.rule: Buy at a new 55-day closing high above the 200-day average. Sell at a close under the lowest close of the previous 20 days.

rules.name: Three down days
rules.rule: Buy after three lower closes in a row above the 200-day average. Sell at the first higher close or after 5 trading days.

tactical.verdict: 3 of the 4 short-term rules kept a positive average per trade after a 0.25% commission in both halves of the test. Run as a real sleeve of four trades at a time, the best ('Pullback in an uptrend') made 13.8% a year at your broker's 0.25%, -7.1% a year on a 1,000-dollar sleeve once the one-euro minimum applies, and 27.3% a year at a broker with no commission. Short Treasuries pay about 4.8% a year for doing nothing.
tactical.method: Each rule is applied to daily closes of every share and fund on the list. A trade is bought and sold at the close; the result is counted per trade, and the test period is cut in two by date. The sleeve test takes the trades in the order they start, at most four at once, a quarter of the sleeve each, and pays the commission or the minimum fee on every buy and sell.
limits: Closing prices only: real fills differ, and the rules cannot see what happens inside a day.
About four years and one list of shares chosen with hindsight; a rule that passed here can stop working.
No tax, no currency cost and no dividends are included.
The four rules were written down before the test, but testing four and keeping the best still flatters the winner.
